sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Nobody publishes a map of the 1947 area codes. What exists is a map of today's area codes, a list of the original 77, and a long history of which code was carved out of which. To color the country by how fast a code was to dial in 1947, those three things had to be stitched into one dataset.

The whole thing runs as a small pipeline: five scripts that download the public sources, clean them, work out the history, check the result and hand one set of files to the map, the poster and the film. Run it again and you get the same map.

sections.heading: Where the shapes come from
paragraphs: The polygons are the area code boundaries as of October 2015, from a dataset UCLA's map library published and a GitHub user republished as GeoJSON. They are detailed down to the street, which is more than a national map needs, so they are simplified to about a kilometer and a half and clipped to the coastline and the Great Lakes.
That file is the only geometry the map ever uses. Every earlier year is built from it.

sections.heading: Going back in time
paragraphs: Each area code has a parent: the code it was split out of, and the year it happened. 718 was cut from 212 in 1984; 347 was added on top of 718 in 1999. Written down for all 425 codes, that is a family tree with 86 roots, the original 1947 codes.

With the tree, any year is a question of walking upward. Take a 2015 territory, follow its parents back until you reach a code that already existed in the year you want, and that is the code it carried. Territories that land on the same code are merged into one shape. Do this for 1947 and the 237 modern territories collapse into the 77 originals; do it for 1960 and you get 101.

From 1992 the phone companies started adding codes on top of existing territory instead of dividing it. Those overlays never changed a boundary, so the map shows them as hatching rather than new shapes. The last boundary change was in 2007, which is why the year slider can run to 2025 on 2015 polygons.

sections.heading: Making the edges line up
paragraphs: The 2015 file looked clean and was not. Where two area codes met, each side had its own slightly different copy of the shared edge, sometimes a few kilometers apart. Merging neighbors across those edges produced spikes and slivers, and a few places (Phoenix, for one) rendered as holes.

The fix was to treat all 237 polygons as one surface rather than 237 separate shapes: snap the shared edges together so both sides use the same line, merge away slivers narrower than three kilometers, and simplify the shared edges once instead of once per side. Shapely added exactly these tools in 2025, and they turned a day of hand repairs into one function call.

sections.heading: Counting people
paragraphs: The usual story is that the busiest places got the quickest codes. To put that next to the map, each 1947 territory needed a population. The Census Bureau publishes every county's population for every census since 1900. Each county is assigned to the 1947 territory that contains its center, and the counts are summed. The 77 territories add up to 150.7 million people, which is the 1950 Census count for the 48 states, so nobody was lost on the way.
A code's clicks are just its digits added up, with 0 counted as ten: 212 is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5, and 605 is 6 + 10 + 5 = 21. The chart below puts the two together for all 77.

sections.heading: Checking the work
paragraphs: Three checks run every time the data is rebuilt. The number of codes in service each year is compared with the telephone numbering authority's own records, for twelve years between 1947 and 2025; all twelve match. The 77 reconstructed originals have to cover the whole of the lower 48. And every shape has to close cleanly in the browser, because an open ring is what draws as a spike.
One map engine draws the interactive map on this page, the poster, and every frame of the film, so the three never disagree.

gaps: The 1947 map is rebuilt from today's territories. Where a 1947 boundary ran along a line no later code followed, the 1947 shape is approximate, and three codes that were split from two parents each (607, 608 and 806) are drawn wholly inside their main parent.
Slivers narrower than three kilometers between neighboring codes were merged into the neighbor with the longer shared edge.
Connecticut's 1950 population is the state total, because Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022 and the 1950 table does not know them.
Canada's nine original codes are in the family tree but not on the map, which covers the lower 48 states.

Whether short codes were deliberately given to the busiest places is disputed. The pattern in the assignments and the 1950 populations is what the map shows; the reason is the usual account, not a documented one.
credit: The format, a map of an everyday numbering rule with a short film and the method published beside it, follows Alan McConchie's Voronoi Highways (2025). The map engine, the data pipeline and the film are this piece's own.
